status_summary: USTR released a WTO reform paper on 2026-03-23 (WT/GC/W/998), building on a December 2025 paper, that proposes objective criteria for who may use special and differential treatment, citing as an example the 2019 US criteria under which OECD members or applicants, G20 members, high-income economies and members with at least 0.5 percent of world merchandise trade would forgo it; the paper says China's September 2025 pledge raises questions and that China should never again be eligible for such treatment in a WTO agreement. China announced on 2025-09-23 that it would not seek new special and differential treatment in WTO negotiations while keeping its developing-country status, a decision by China rather than a US action. China's self-declared status has not changed, and no WTO decision on eligibility criteria was found. H.Res. 687, a non-binding House resolution (introduced 2025-09-09 per a bill tracker) urging that the UN stop classifying China as developing, was referred to committee.

timeline.event: China's Premier announced that China will not seek new special and differential treatment in WTO negotiations while remaining a developing country.
USTR issued a paper on WTO reform, the first of two reform papers listed on its WTO reform page.

title: End China's developing-nation status in the WTO and other international bodies
uncertainties: The March 2026 paper was read; the December 2025 paper was listed on USTR's page but not opened, so its event text is limited to its existence. The paper does not state China's developing status directly; its China points are in paragraphs 16 to 20 and a footnote. The H.Res. 687 details come from a bill tracker because congress.gov blocked the fetch, and its sponsor was not identified. Other international bodies (UN, World Bank) were not searched beyond that resolution. China's pledge is a Chinese decision, not a US action, and does not set the stage.
